title: European defence budgets lift prices before their full output effect appears
summary: When a government signs a contract, producers can respond years before the purchase appears in the national accounts. Cristina Checherita-Westphal and Laust L. Særkjær show how much that distinction matters for interpreting European defence budgets. Dating the capital component closer to the order shifts the peak estimated output multiplier from around the first year to the third or fourth. Consumer prices respond earlier. The paper thus offers a reason why an immediate comparison between a budget increase and recorded GDP can miss part of the adjustment, even if the eventual increase in domestic output is modest.

The authors follow up to 27 EU economies from 1999 to 2025 in the baseline. They use panel local projections to estimate cumulative changes in output, expenditure components and prices over five years, scaling quantities by lagged trend GDP. European accounts record major capital purchases on delivery. To approximate when they were ordered, the authors move capital spending back by a country-specific median delay measured from historical international equipment transactions. Table A.2.1 puts the median across countries at two years, with individual lags from zero to four. Exports help proxy domestic production times because the underlying transaction data omit domestic orders. Other categories of spending retain their original dates.

Figures 3 and 4 trace increases in total spending equivalent to 1% of trend GDP. Both estimates of the output multiplier peak near one euro per euro spent. By year five the unadjusted estimate is about 0.3 and the adjusted estimate about 0.6. The adjustment also removes recent observations for which deliveries have yet to be recorded. Figure A.2.3 compares both measures on identical observations and confirms that moving expenditure toward the order date delays the peak. Extending the unadjusted series through the latest years changes its magnitude substantially. The short history of the recent expansion cannot distinguish a genuinely smaller multiplier from output that has yet to materialise.

For monetary policymakers, the price estimates are more precise than many of the output estimates. In the adjusted specification, cumulative HICP inflation is about one percentage point higher by year one, peaks around 1.4 points in year three and remains about 1.25 points higher at year five. These figures measure accumulated changes in inflation over the horizon. They do not represent an extra 1.4 percentage points of annual inflation in each year. Ending the sample in 2021 reduces the peak. The GDP deflator also incorporates government production costs directly, which helps explain differences between its response and the consumer price response.

Budget composition changes the interpretation further. Figure 5 attributes the largest output response to capital, for which the estimated consumer price response is much smaller and imprecise. Personnel expenditure raises household consumption and prices, while private investment falls. Intermediate purchases produce a pronounced decline in net exports at longer horizons. Figure 6 gives budget planners a second calculation: each extra euro of capital purchases is associated with roughly 30 cents of cumulative personnel and intermediate expenditure over five years. The combined response becomes statistically significant from year four. In Figure 7 the high-debt group shows a weaker output response than the low-debt group, but the estimates are too uncertain to assign a country a reliable multiplier from its debt ratio alone. The authors’ evidence is strongest on the timing of transmission and the differing price and recurrent-cost implications of the spending mix.

questions.question: Would national contract records change the estimated time profile of GDP and inflation?
questions.detail: The adjustment applies a historical country median to all capital purchases, although delivery times plausibly differ across projects and periods. Linking dated budget commitments, payments and deliveries to the accounts would permit a direct comparison on an identical sample. If the estimated output peak moves again, one could isolate how much of the current result comes from assigning a common lag within each country. This matters for the timing of growth-sensitive exposures. National procurement accounts and treasury payment records would be the starting point.

questions.question: Does the inflation response to personnel expenditure reflect wages paid to existing workers or growth in public employment?
questions.detail: Separate wage settlements from headcount changes, then trace comparable pay, vacancies and consumer prices across regions with different initial exposure. Divergent responses would help explain both the strong price estimates and the decline in private investment in Figure 5, which the authors identify as an unresolved feature. Public payroll records and official regional price and labour-market data would help assess which indicator gives early warning of inflation persistence.

questions.question: Has the domestic output return on the post-2022 increase changed once later deliveries are observed?
questions.detail: Revisit the matched-sample exercise as the missing years become available. Compare episodes with similar capital shares and debt positions but different import shares, tracing consumption, net exports and output together. A persistent gap after orders have been delivered would give more weight to a change in domestic demand transmission than to incomplete observation of the latest spending cycle. Revised national accounts and trade data, alongside the transaction series used by the authors, would help calibrate medium-term growth exposures.

limitation: The order dates are approximations constructed from historical international transactions. The latest adjusted observations are unavailable for countries with longer delivery lags, and uncertainty around the output and debt-state estimates is substantial.
